title: Anytime-CBU: Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Consequence-Based Utility Scoring

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution aims to reduce the computational cost of Consequence-Based Utility (CBU) scoring by addressing inefficiencies in uniform rollout allocation, which wastes compute on candidates whose quality is clear after few rollouts. Prior paper [19] explicitly formulates test-time search as a resource allocation problem and derives an optimal strategy to maximize the probability of obtaining the best result under a fixed rollout budget. This aligns with the purpose of reducing computational cost in test-time scaling by optimizing rollout allocation. Therefore, the purpose is **covered** by [19].

### Mechanism
The contribution reformulates CBU scoring as a best-arm identification (BAI) problem and applies LUCB-style adaptive allocation with Beta-posterior confidence bounds, arm elimination, and early stopping. Prior papers [1], [4], [6], [7], [8], [9], and [27] all address BAI problems and propose LUCB-style algorithms with adaptive confidence bounds, arm elimination, and early stopping. For example, [4] generalizes the LUCB algorithm for linearly parameterized bandits, while [6] introduces a novel arm elimination scheme with adaptive confidence bounds. These mechanisms are substantively equivalent to the contribution's mechanism, as they share the same underlying primitives (LUCB-style adaptive allocation, arm elimination, and early stopping). Therefore, the mechanism is **covered** by [4], [6], [7], [8], [9], and [27].

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates Anytime-CBU on RealMath with two solver models (Qwen2.5-Math-7B and DeepSeek-R1-7B) against Uniform-CBU. Prior papers [10], [13], [14], and [19] evaluate test-time compute optimization methods for LLM reasoning tasks using similar evaluation designs, including comparisons against baseline methods (e.g., uniform allocation) and performance metrics on mathematical reasoning tasks. For example, [19] evaluates its optimal rollout allocation strategy on test-time scaling for LLM reasoning tasks, which is substantively equivalent to the evaluation design used in the contribution. Therefore, the evaluation is **covered** by [10], [13], [14], and [19].

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM evaluation and test-time compute for mathematical reasoning. Prior papers [10], [13], [14], and [19] also address LLM evaluation and test-time compute optimization for reasoning tasks, including mathematical reasoning. For example, [13] focuses on improving LLM reasoning quality in mathematical domains, and [14] introduces a metric for answer stabilization in test-time reasoning algorithms for LLMs. These papers clearly operate in the same general application area. Therefore, the domain is **covered** by [10], [13], [14], and [19].

## Purpose

The purpose is to reduce computational cost of CBU scoring by avoiding wasted compute on candidates whose quality is clear after few rollouts — i.e., adaptive allocation to avoid uniform waste in a rollout-based scoring system.

- Paper [16] (VIP): "allocates a given rollout budget to the prompts" adaptively for RL training, addressing "uniform allocation implicitly treats all prompts as equally informative." This is about training-time rollout allocation, not test-time CBU scoring.
- Paper [19] (Every Rollout Counts): "formulate test-time search as a resource allocation problem and derive the optimal allocation strategy" — very close, about efficient test-time scaling via optimal rollout allocation.
- Paper [17] (OptPO): "adaptively allocates inference budgets" for test-time policy optimization, addressing "fixed-budget majority voting" redundancy.
- Paper [14] (Certaindex): addresses "wastefully generate many tokens without improving accuracy" at test time.
- Paper [13]: "early rejection" to reduce compute in reasoning with PRMs.

Paper [19] most directly covers the purpose: reducing wasted compute from uniform rollout allocation at test time by adaptive allocation. Paper [17] (OptPO) also covers this — "fixed-budget majority voting to estimate rewards, incurring substantial computational redundancy" and proposes adaptive allocation. Both cover the purpose at the problem-class level.

## Mechanism

The mechanism is: reformulate scoring as a BAI problem, apply LUCB-style adaptive allocation with Beta-posterior confidence bounds, arm elimination, and early stopping.

- Paper [27] (AT-LUCB): introduces "AT-LUCB (AnyTime Lower and Upper Confidence Bound)" for anytime explore-m in MAB — directly uses LUCB-style adaptive allocation with anytime properties. This is the closest match to the LUCB-style mechanism.
- Papers [1], [4], [7], [8], [11]: all use LUCB-style algorithms for BAI with confidence bounds and arm elimination.
- Paper [17] (OptPO): "formulating the voting process as a Bayesian sequential probability ratio test" with Beta posteriors — uses Beta-posterior confidence bounds for adaptive stopping in rollout allocation. This is very close to the mechanism described.
- Paper [19]: derives optimal allocation for test-time search as resource allocation, but doesn't specifically use LUCB/BAI framing.
- Paper [33] (Faster Hoeffding Racing): Bernstein races for arm elimination — covers arm elimination with confidence bounds.

Paper [27] covers LUCB-style adaptive allocation with anytime properties. Paper [17] covers Beta-posterior confidence bounds with early stopping for rollout allocation. Paper [8]/[31] covers KL-LUCB with anytime confidence bounds. The combination of BAI + LUCB + Beta posteriors + arm elimination + early stopping applied to rollout scoring is most directly covered by [27] (LUCB anytime) and [17] (Beta posteriors for rollout allocation).

## Evaluation

The evaluation uses RealMath benchmark with two solver models (Qwen2.5-Math-7B, DeepSeek-R1-7B) compared against Uniform-CBU baseline.

- Paper [10]: evaluates LLM test-time compute scaling on math benchmarks with multiple models — same design (math benchmark + multiple LLM models + baseline comparison).
- Paper [19]: evaluates test-time scaling on math reasoning benchmarks with LLM models.
- Paper [14]: evaluates on reasoning benchmarks with LLM models.
- Paper [16]: evaluates rollout allocation with math reasoning models.

The evaluation design (math reasoning benchmark + multiple LLM solver models + comparison against uniform baseline) is covered by papers [10], [16], [19] which all use the same evaluation design in the LLM math reasoning space.

## Domain

The domain is LLM evaluation / test-time compute for mathematical reasoning.

- Paper [10]: "scaling of inference-time computation in LLMs" for challenging prompts — directly in test-time compute for LLM reasoning.
- Paper [14]: test-time reasoning algorithms for LLMs.
- Paper [16]: test-time rollout allocation for LLM reasoning.
- Paper [19]: test-time scaling for LLM reasoning.

This domain is clearly covered by multiple papers [10], [14], [16], [19].
